title: HTTP/3
subtitle: HTTP over QUIC — eliminating head-of-line blocking with UDP-based transport
summary: HTTP/3 is HTTP mapped onto QUIC instead of TCP. Each request and response uses its own QUIC stream, so a lost packet delays only that stream, and HTTP/3 adds a small set of frame types plus QPACK for header compression. The meaning of requests and responses is unchanged from RFC 9110, and connections start with the faster QUIC handshake.

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP/3 is HTTP carried over QUIC instead of TCP. Each request and response uses its own QUIC stream, so a lost packet delays only that stream. HTTP/3 adds a small set of frame types and QPACK header compression. The meaning of requests and responses is unchanged from RFC 9110, and connections start with the faster QUIC handshake.

questions: how is http/3 different from http/2
how does a browser find out a server supports http/3

tldr.problem: HTTP/2 multiplexes requests on one TCP connection, so a single lost packet stalls every request until it is retransmitted.
tldr.mechanism: HTTP/3 maps each request and response onto its own QUIC stream, uses a few frame types for HTTP-specific data, and compresses headers with QPACK.
tldr.outcome: Lost packets block only the stream they belong to, and connections set up faster and survive network changes.

facts.label: Discovery
facts.value: Alt-Svc header or HTTP/2 ALTSVC frame

today: HTTP/3 is supported by all major browsers and by large CDNs and web services. Servers such as nginx and Caddy and libraries such as curl can speak it. Browsers usually learn about it from an Alt-Svc header on an earlier HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 connection and fall back to TCP when UDP is blocked.

implementations.note: Command-line client and libcurl with HTTP/3 support.

implementations.note: Web server with HTTP/3 enabled by default.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP/3 is the third major version of HTTP. It uses QUIC (RFC 9000) as its transport protocol instead of TCP, fundamentally changing how HTTP data moves across the network.

HTTP/3 addresses a major performance bottleneck of HTTP/2: TCP-level head-of-line blocking. Since QUIC provides independent streams at the transport layer, a lost packet only affects the stream it belongs to.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP/3 is the third major version of HTTP. It uses QUIC (RFC 9000) instead of TCP as its transport. This fixes a bottleneck in HTTP/2, TCP head-of-line blocking, where one lost packet delays all data. QUIC provides independent streams, so a lost packet affects only its own stream.

sections.title: QUIC Transport
sections.content:
HTTP/3 relies entirely on QUIC for transport, which provides:

Stream Multiplexing
QUIC natively supports multiplexed streams, so HTTP/3 does not need to implement its own multiplexing layer. Each HTTP request/response uses an independent QUIC stream.
Built-in Encryption
QUIC integrates TLS 1.3, so every HTTP/3 connection is encrypted by default. There is no unencrypted mode.
Connection Migration
QUIC connections survive IP address changes (e.g., switching from Wi-Fi to cellular), since connections are identified by connection IDs rather than IP/port tuples.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP/3 relies on QUIC for transport. QUIC already provides multiplexed streams, so HTTP/3 needs no multiplexing of its own and uses one QUIC stream per request. QUIC includes TLS 1.3, so every HTTP/3 connection is encrypted. Connection IDs let a connection survive IP address changes, such as a move from Wi-Fi to cellular.

sections.title: Connection Setup
sections.content:
HTTP/3 connection setup is significantly faster than HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 over TCP+TLS:

Protocol Stack
Round Trips Before the Request Is Sent
HTTP/1.1 over TCP + TLS 1.2
3 RTT (TCP 1 + TLS 1.2 2)
HTTP/2 over TCP + TLS 1.3
2 RTT (TCP 1 + TLS 1.3 1)
HTTP/3 over QUIC
1 RTT (combined QUIC and TLS handshake)
HTTP/3 over QUIC (0-RTT)
0 RTT (resumed connection)

0-RTT data is vulnerable to replay attacks. Servers must ensure that 0-RTT requests are idempotent (e.g., GET requests) and implement replay protection for sensitive operations.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP/3 sets up connections faster than earlier versions over TCP and TLS. Before the first request, HTTP/1.1 with TLS 1.2 needs 3 round trips, HTTP/2 with TLS 1.3 needs 2, and HTTP/3 needs 1. A resumed connection can use 0-RTT, but that data is open to replay attacks. Servers must ensure 0-RTT requests are idempotent, such as GET.

sections.title: HTTP Framing
sections.content:
HTTP/3 uses a simpler framing layer than HTTP/2, since QUIC handles stream management:

0x0DATA — Request/response body data
0x1HEADERS — Compressed header fields (QPACK)
0x3CANCEL_PUSH — Cancel a server push
0x4SETTINGS — Connection configuration
0x5PUSH_PROMISE — Server push announcement
0x7GOAWAY — Graceful connection shutdown

HTTP/3 uses QPACK instead of HPACK for header compression. QPACK is designed for QUIC's out-of-order delivery model, avoiding the head-of-line blocking that HPACK would cause on QUIC streams.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP/3 uses a simpler framing layer than HTTP/2 because QUIC manages streams. Frame types include DATA for body data, HEADERS for compressed header fields, SETTINGS, GOAWAY and the server push frames. Headers are compressed with QPACK rather than HPACK, because QPACK suits QUIC's out-of-order delivery and avoids head-of-line blocking.

sections.title: Request/Response
sections.content:
HTTP/3 requests and responses use the same semantics as all other HTTP versions (RFC 9110). The differences are in how they are transported:

One Stream Per Request
Each request/response pair uses a single bidirectional QUIC stream. Streams are fully independent — there is no ordering between different requests.
No Head-of-Line Blocking
If a packet carrying data for Stream A is lost, only Stream A is blocked while awaiting retransmission. Streams B and C continue unimpeded.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP/3 requests and responses mean the same as in other HTTP versions (RFC 9110). Each request and response pair uses one bidirectional QUIC stream, and streams are independent, with no ordering between requests. If a packet for one stream is lost, only that stream waits for retransmission, and the others continue.

sections.title: Server Push
sections.content:
HTTP/3 retains server push from HTTP/2, with modifications for the QUIC transport:

Push Streams
Server push responses are sent on unidirectional QUIC streams, prefixed with a push ID that correlates to a PUSH_PROMISE sent on the request stream.
Client Control
A server cannot push until the client sends a MAX_PUSH_ID frame, so a client that never sends one disables server push entirely. Clients can also use CANCEL_PUSH to reject individual push promises before the data is sent.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP/3 keeps server push from HTTP/2. Pushed responses travel on unidirectional QUIC streams, tagged with a push ID that matches a PUSH_PROMISE on the request stream. A server cannot push until the client sends a MAX_PUSH_ID frame, so a client that never sends one disables push. A client can reject a single push with CANCEL_PUSH.
